name: Katalin Karikó
setback: For more than two decades at the University of Pennsylvania, Karikó worked in non-tenured positions. She repeatedly failed to win the research funding her work needed, was turned down for a tenure-track post, and was rebuffed again when she later sought tenure.
after: Frustrated, she left Penn in 2013 to join the German company BioNTech. In 2023 she and Drew Weissman were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work on modified mRNA.
reflection: For years, the way her institution measured her work was funding. That measure said something about the system at the time, not about the worth of the person doing the work.

sources.label: Penn refused to give Katalin Karikó tenure. Now she has a Nobel Prize.
Katalin Karikó – Facts

name: Dan Shechtman
setback: Shechtman observed a crystal structure that, according to the accepted rules of the time, should not have been possible. His discovery was strongly contested, and while defending his findings he was asked to leave his research group.
after: His observations of what are now called quasicrystals were recognised with the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
reflection: Being told you are wrong by people around you is painful, and it is not the same thing as being wrong. Either way, it is not a verdict on who you are.

sources.label: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2011 – Press release

name: Barry Marshall
setback: Marshall proposed that a bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, plays a role in stomach disease. In his own account, by 1984 most of his work was being rejected for publication, accepted papers were delayed, and he faced constant criticism that his conclusions were premature.
after: He kept working on the question. In 2005 he and Robin Warren were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering the bacterium's role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.
reflection: A run of rejections can feel personal. It is often a description of where a field is at a given moment, and it never measures your value as a person.

sources.label: Barry J. Marshall – Biographical
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2005 – Summary

name: Jocelyn Bell Burnell
setback: As a graduate student at Cambridge in the 1960s, Bell Burnell lived with impostor syndrome: a fear that she was not good enough and would be thrown out. When she spotted an unusual signal in her telescope data, it then disappeared.
after: She kept taking and checking data until the signal returned about a month later; it led to the discovery of pulsars. The 1974 Nobel Prize connected to that research went to her supervisor, not to her. In 2018 she received the Breakthrough Prize and donated the $3 million award to fund physics scholarships for students from under-represented groups.
reflection: Feeling like an impostor is not evidence that you are one. Many careful, capable people carry that feeling quietly.

sources.label: In 1974, They Gave The Nobel To Her Supervisor. Now She's Won A $3 Million Prize
Interview with Jocelyn Bell Burnell on impostor syndrome

name: John Gurdon
setback: At about fifteen, Gurdon was ranked last in his school's biology year. His teacher wrote a damning report, and he was taken off science altogether and moved to classics and modern languages.
after: Oxford accepted him on the condition that he would not study classics. After a preparatory year of basic science, he was allowed into zoology. In 2012 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for showing that mature cells can be reprogrammed.
reflection: Someone else's early judgement of what you can do is only that: one judgement, made at one moment.

The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2012 – Summary
Nobel Prize Winner Proves Teacher Wrong

name: Hans Krebs
setback: In 1933 Krebs was dismissed from his post at the University of Freiburg under the Nazi regime and moved to England. In 1937 the journal Nature declined his paper on what became known as the citric acid cycle, saying it already had enough material for the coming weeks.
after: The paper was published instead in the Dutch journal Enzymologia. In 1953 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering the citric acid cycle.
reflection: Sometimes a door closes for reasons that have nothing to do with the quality of what you brought to it.

name: Peter Higgs
setback: In July 1964 Higgs submitted a paper to the journal Physics Letters, and the editor turned it down. He was annoyed by the rejection.
after: He revised the paper, adding a prediction of a new particle, and it was published in Physical Review Letters in October 1964. That particle is now called the Higgs boson; he shared the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physics.
reflection: A rejection can sting and still not be the last word on your work. It was one editor's decision, on one day.

sources.label: Higgs owes his Nobel to an editor and a biologist
Peter W. Higgs – Biographical

name: Barbara McClintock
setback: When McClintock presented her findings on 'jumping genes' (transposition) in 1951, the talk did not go well, and other scientists largely ignored her work for more than a decade. She stopped publishing detailed reports, though she kept working.
after: In the 1960s other researchers found transposition in bacteria and other organisms. In 1983 she received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, more than thirty years after the work it honoured.
reflection: Recognition can be slow, uneven, or absent. Your work and your worth exist whether or not anyone is paying attention yet.

name: Tu Youyou
setback: Tu joined a national search for new malaria treatments in which thousands of compounds had already been screened without finding a useful medicine. In her own work, early leads were dropped, and extracts of the plant qinghao gave results that were inconsistent and could not be reproduced. In her words, there were multiple experiments and failures.
after: She went back to the historical Chinese medical literature. An ancient text describing how the plant was prepared led her to suspect that heat might be destroying its active components, so she redesigned the extraction to work at a lower temperature, which produced an effective extract. The work led to artemisinin, and she shared the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
reflection: An experiment that does not work is not a failure of the person running it. Most research is made of attempts that don't work.

sources.label: Tu Youyou – Biographical

name: Venki Ramakrishnan
setback: During his physics PhD, Ramakrishnan felt for the first time in years that he had chosen the wrong field, and decided to switch to biology. Many graduate programs would not accept someone who already had a PhD; his one interview did not lead to a place. Later, applying for faculty positions, he did not get a single interview.
after: He retrained in biology and went on to study the structure of the ribosome, work for which he shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
reflection: Realising you might be in the wrong place is not the same as having wasted your time. Changing direction is allowed.

sources.label: Venkatraman Ramakrishnan – Biographical
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2009 – Summary

name: Carol Greider
setback: Greider has dyslexia. As a child she was placed in remedial classes and felt she wasn't as good as the other kids. Later, her graduate entrance test scores were low, and most of the programs she applied to turned her down.
after: Caltech and UC Berkeley looked past the scores. At Berkeley, working with Elizabeth Blackburn, she discovered the enzyme telomerase as a graduate student in 1984, work that was recognised with the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
reflection: A test score, a label, or a difficult start describes one part of a situation. It does not describe the whole of you.

sources.label: Carol Greider, Ph.D.
Carol Greider – Women who changed science

name: Andrew Wiles
setback: In 1993, after years of work on the problem, Wiles announced a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem. An error was then found in a crucial part of the argument, one subtle enough that he had not noticed it.
after: After about a year of further work, and with help from the Cambridge mathematician Richard Taylor, he repaired the proof.
reflection: Finding a flaw in something you have poured yourself into is hard. It does not erase the work you did, or the person who did it.

sources.label: Andrew Wiles on Solving Fermat

name: Stanley B. Prusiner
setback: When Prusiner argued that scrapie and related diseases were caused by infectious proteins, which he called prions, many virologists did not believe him and some researchers in the field were angry. He wrote that even modest NIH support was hard to get, and UCSF at one point told him he would not get tenure.
after: The tenure decision was reversed and he kept working. As prions became more widely accepted, his work was recognised with many prizes, including the 1997 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, which he received alone.
reflection: Being disbelieved by your own field is painful. It says nothing about your value as a person.

sources.label: Stanley B. Prusiner – Biographical
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1997 – Summary

name: Alfred Wegener
setback: Wegener proposed that the continents move. Most geologists dismissed the idea as a fairy tale, many attacks were aimed at him personally, and he could not get a professorship at any German university. He died on an expedition in Greenland long before his idea was accepted.
after: From the mid-1950s, new evidence convinced most scientists that continents do move. Plate tectonics is now almost universally accepted, and NASA notes that Wegener was right in most of his major concepts.
reflection: Sometimes people don't see the value of an idea while its author is there to hear it. That never made the thinking, or the person, worth less.

sources.label: Alfred Wegener

name: Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin
setback: In her 1925 doctoral thesis, Payne found that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium, against the prevailing view. A senior astronomer contradicted her, and she added a line to her published thesis calling her own result almost certainly not real. At Harvard she was not acknowledged as a faculty member for many years.
after: She stayed at Harvard until she retired in 1966. In 1956 she became the first woman promoted to full professor at Harvard, and the first woman to chair a department there.
reflection: Being pushed to doubt your own work can shake you. It doesn't change what you saw, or who you are.

sources.label: Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin

name: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar
setback: As a young researcher, Chandrasekhar worked out a maximum mass for white dwarf stars. At a Royal Astronomical Society meeting in January 1935, the famous astronomer Arthur Eddington spoke right after him and ridiculed the underlying idea. The attack came as a total surprise to him.
after: He went on to a long career in astrophysics. In 1983 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for his theoretical studies of the structure and evolution of stars.
reflection: Public criticism from someone you look up to can hurt deeply. It is one person's judgement of an idea, not a measure of you.

About Chandra: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar
The Nobel Prize in Physics 1983 – Summary

name: Peter Mitchell
setback: Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory of how cells transfer energy was at first received with scepticism. Separately, illness led him to resign from Edinburgh University in 1963, and he stepped away from research for a while.
after: He restored Glynn House in Cornwall, set up a laboratory there, and with Jennifer Moyle founded Glynn Research, starting work in 1965. His theory became generally accepted, and he received the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
reflection: Illness and doubt can force a pause or a change of direction. Neither decides what a person is worth.

name: Donna Strickland
setback: After her PhD in optics in 1989, it took Strickland eight years to find a full-time university position, partly because of the difficulty of fitting two academic careers into one household. She was still an associate professor when she won the Nobel Prize; she says she simply never applied for full professor.
after: The University of Waterloo hired her in 1997, where she later became associate chair of physics. In 2018 she shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for a method of generating high-intensity, ultra-short laser pulses.
reflection: A slow or unusual career path is not a verdict on your ability. Titles and timelines don't measure a person.

Donna Strickland – Facts

name: Shinya Yamanaka
setback: Training as an orthopaedic surgeon, Yamanaka found his skills weaker than he expected; one operation took him two hours where others needed thirty minutes, and he lost confidence. After moving into research, he had little funding, journals rejected his work, and he felt lonely and depressed.
after: He came close to giving up science, but kept going and later got his first own laboratory as an associate professor. He shared the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for showing that mature cells can be reprogrammed.
reflection: Not being good at the first path you chose says nothing about what you are worth. It may only mean your place is somewhere else.

sources.label: Shinya Yamanaka – Biographical
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2012 – Summary

name: Paul Nurse
setback: Nurse kept failing his French exam. Without a foreign language qualification, which every university entrant needed, he could not start a degree, so he worked as a technician in a microbiology laboratory linked to a local brewery.
after: A professor at Birmingham interviewed him and arranged for his weakness in languages to be overlooked. Nurse later did a PhD and shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering key regulators of the cell cycle.
reflection: One exam you cannot pass is not a measure of your whole mind. A closed door can say more about the rules than about you.

sources.label: Paul Nurse – Biographical
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2001 – Summary

name: Mario Capecchi
setback: In 1980 Capecchi asked the US National Institutes of Health to fund experiments on targeting genes in mammalian cells. The reviewers judged the idea not worth pursuing and refused. Much earlier, as a small child in wartime Italy, he had at times lived on the streets.
after: He started the experiments anyway. By 1984 they were clearly working, and when he applied again the reviewers approved the grant. He shared the 2007 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for methods of modifying specific genes in mice.
reflection: When others doubt an idea, that is a judgement about the idea at one moment, not about the person holding it.

Mario R. Capecchi – Biographical
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2007 – Summary

name: Robert G. Edwards
setback: Early on, the human eggs Edwards fertilised in the laboratory never developed beyond a single cell division. In 1971, amid resistance to the research from society and the scientific establishment, the UK Medical Research Council decided to stop supporting his work with Patrick Steptoe.
after: Private funding kept the project going. In 1978 the first baby conceived through in vitro fertilisation was born, and in 2010 Edwards received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for developing IVF.
reflection: Losing support for your work is painful. It does not erase the worth of the questions you care about, or of you.

sources.label: Speed read: Making mothers of invention
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2010 – Summary

name: Rita Levi-Montalcini
setback: Under Mussolini's racial laws, Levi-Montalcini was barred from an academic career. During the war her family later had to flee to Florence, where they lived in hiding until the war ended.
after: Unable to work at a university, she built a small research unit in her bedroom. After the war she resumed her university position in Turin, later moved to St. Louis, and shared the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering growth factors.
reflection: Being shut out by unjust rules reflects on those rules, never on your worth or your right to be curious.

sources.label: Rita Levi-Montalcini – Biographical
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1986 – Summary

name: Gertrude B. Elion
setback: During the Depression, Elion applied to universities for graduate funding but could not go on to graduate school, and the few laboratory jobs were not open to women. She taught, worked as a lab assistant and did quality control for a food company. Later she was told she could not continue a doctorate part-time.
after: She earned a master's degree in 1941, became assistant to George Hitchings, and chose to keep that job rather than pursue the doctorate. She shared the 1988 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries of important principles of drug treatment.
reflection: Missing a credential or an opening does not measure your ability. Your worth was never decided by who let you in.

sources.label: Gertrude B. Elion – Biographical
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1988 – Summary

name: Melanie Stefan
setback: Like most researchers, Stefan applied for many grants that she did not get; for a while she kept a spreadsheet of every one. When she first wrote about the idea of a CV of failures in Nature in 2010, as a postdoc, she says nothing happened.
after: Her essay suggested that keeping a visible record of rejected applications can help others deal with setbacks. The idea later spread widely. She says the spreadsheet shows her how much she has worked. She went on to become a professor at MSB Medical School Berlin.
reflection: A list of rejections is also a record of effort. The applications that didn't work out say nothing about how much you are worth.

sources.label: Embracing failure in art and science
A CV of failures

name: Johannes Haushofer
setback: Haushofer, then a professor of psychology and public affairs at Princeton, had faced many rejections that felt huge at the time: degree programmes he did not get into, including a PhD programme in Stockholm and graduate medicine courses at Cambridge and UCL, plus positions and fellowships he did not get.
after: Inspired by Melanie Stefan's essay in Nature, he published a CV of failures to balance the visible record of successes. It drew far more attention than anything else he had done, which he found amusing.
reflection: Most failures stay invisible while successes are on display. The rejections behind someone are part of an ordinary research life.

sources.label: When A Resume Of Failures Becomes A Recipe For Success
CV of Failures

name: Lise Meitner
setback: In July 1938 Meitner had to flee Nazi Germany without a valid passport, carrying only hand luggage. A few months later her long-time colleague Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann discovered nuclear fission. The Nobel Prize for that discovery later went to Hahn alone.
after: Hahn told Meitner about the result, and from exile she worked out the theory that explained it, together with her nephew.
reflection: Being forced to start over, and being left out of recognition, does not erase what a person contributed or who they are.

sources.label: Lise Meitner flees to Stockholm

name: Chien-Shiung Wu
setback: In 1956 and 1957 Wu led the experiment showing that parity is violated in beta decay. The 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics went to the theorists Chen Ning Yang and Tsung-Dao Lee; neither Wu nor anyone else who had measured the effect had been nominated that year.
after: From 1958 until her death in 1997 she was nominated for the Nobel Prize at least seven times, with support from several laureates. She never received it.
reflection: Recognition is not always given fairly, or at all. The value of careful, brilliant work does not depend on a prize.

sources.label: Overlooked for the Nobel: Chien-Shiung Wu

name: Svante Pääbo
setback: As a PhD student, Pääbo tried to extract DNA from Egyptian mummies on the side, without telling his advisor. Later he and his colleagues found that contamination was a major difficulty: the tiniest particle of dust from human skin could ruin a result.
after: The mummy work was published in a small East German journal in 1984 and a year later in Nature. To deal with contamination he turned to DNA from extinct animals such as mammoths. In 2022 he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on the genomes of extinct hominins.
reflection: Sometimes the method itself fights back and progress means stepping sideways for a while. That is not a sign you don't belong.

sources.label: Svante Pääbo, 2013 Genetics Prize
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2022 – Summary

name: Shirley Ann Jackson
setback: As a first-year student at MIT, Jackson asked to join a study group of other first-year women working on physics problems and was told to go away. Students avoided sitting next to her in lectures. She described those years as pretty isolating, and after the study group turned her away she went back to her room and cried.
after: She told herself she still had to hand in the problem sets, and finished the work. In 1973 she became the first African-American woman to earn a doctorate at MIT. She later worked at Bell Labs, chaired the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission and led Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute.
reflection: Being shut out by others says more about them than about you. Feeling alone in a place does not mean you don't belong there.

sources.label: The remarkable career of Shirley Ann Jackson

name: Rosalyn Yalow
setback: Rosalyn Yalow and Solomon Berson submitted their findings on insulin antibodies to Science and to The Journal of Clinical Investigation, and both journals turned the paper down. Reviewers objected to their use of the term insulin antibody.
after: They changed the wording to describe an insulin-binding globulin, and JCI published the paper in 1956. Yalow later received the 1977 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for developing radioimmunoassay, and she showed the old rejection letter during her Nobel Lecture.
reflection: Having to rework how you describe your own findings can feel like losing ground. A rejected manuscript is a judgement on one draft, not on the person who wrote it.

name: Paul Lauterbur
setback: When Paul Lauterbur first submitted his paper on forming images with nuclear magnetic resonance, Nature rejected it. According to NobelPrize.org, the editors were mainly unconvinced by how fuzzy the images were.
after: He appealed, and Nature accepted a revised version that added possible medical uses; it appeared in 1973. Nearly thirty years later the journal publicly celebrated the paper, and Lauterbur shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries concerning MRI.
reflection: Early results are often rough around the edges, and reviewers may not see what you see yet. A rejection can be a reason to explain the work again, not a verdict on its author.

name: Kary Mullis
setback: Kary Mullis, working at a biotech company, wrote up the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for publication. Nature rejected the paper, and Science also declined it, as Mullis himself recalled in his Nobel Lecture.
after: The method paper was eventually published in Methods in Enzymology in 1987. Mullis noted that Science named PCR its Molecule of the Year a few years later, and he shared the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
reflection: Even an idea that later reshapes a field can be turned away by the first journals that see it. Where a paper first lands says little about its worth or yours.

name: Satyendra Nath Bose
setback: While teaching physics at the University of Dhaka, Satyendra Nath Bose sent a paper deriving Planck's radiation law in a new way to the Philosophical Magazine in London. The paper was not published there: one account says it was rejected, another that he never received a reply.
after: In June 1924 he sent the paper to Albert Einstein and asked for help publishing it. Einstein was enthusiastic, saw it as a significant contribution, and had it published in the Zeitschrift für Physik.
reflection: Silence or a no from one journal can feel final, especially far from the main centres of a field. It does not measure the value of the idea or of the person who had it.

name: Enrico Fermi
setback: Around the end of 1933, Enrico Fermi sent a letter to Nature setting out his new theory of beta decay. The editor refused it, reportedly because he thought it contained speculations too remote from physical reality.
after: Fermi published the theory instead in Italian and in the Zeitschrift für Physik. He later considered it his most important contribution to theoretical physics, and C. N. Yang wrote that it sustained the whole field for some forty years.
reflection: Work that feels too bold for one editor can still find its readers elsewhere. One refusal is not a ruling on whether your thinking matters.

name: Lynn Margulis
setback: A few years after her PhD, Lynn Margulis wrote a paper proposing that some structures inside complex cells began as free-living microbes. The manuscript was rejected by 15 journals, and it challenged many scientists' assumptions.
after: The Journal of Theoretical Biology published it in 1967 as On the Origin of Mitosing Cells. The endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts is now generally accepted, though not every organelle she proposed. She later became a Distinguished University Professor at UMass Amherst.
reflection: Fifteen rejections can make anyone question themselves. How many times a paper is turned down says nothing about how much its author is worth.

name: Victor Ambros and Gary Ruvkun
setback: In 1993 Victor Ambros and Gary Ruvkun published their discovery of a tiny regulatory RNA in the worm C. elegans. The Nobel announcement later said the findings were initially met with almost deafening silence, and many researchers saw little relevance for humans or more complex organisms.
after: Seven years passed before a second microRNA, let-7, was found by Ruvkun's lab in 2000; because it is highly conserved, interest in microRNAs grew sharply. The two shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
reflection: Sometimes careful work meets near silence for years. A lack of attention is not the same as a lack of value, in the work or in the people doing it.

name: James P. Allison
setback: After mouse experiments in 1994 suggested that blocking CTLA-4 could help the immune system attack tumours, James Allison spent about five years trying to convince pharmaceutical companies to work with him. He had little success, partly because many earlier immunotherapy trials had failed and the field was sceptical.
after: A colleague persuaded the small biotech company Medarex to take on the project, and it produced the antibody later named ipilimumab. Bristol-Myers Squibb later acquired Medarex and brought the drug to market, and Allison shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
reflection: Years of hearing no from people who could move your work forward is exhausting. Their scepticism reflects the moment and the field, not your worth as a researcher.

name: Ida Noddack
setback: In 1934 Ida Noddack suggested that a bombarded heavy nucleus might break up into several large fragments, years before nuclear fission was widely accepted. Her paper was generally ignored, and her insights were dismissed by contemporaries.
after: Her paper is now seen as one of the earliest expressions of the idea of nuclear fission.
reflection: Being early can look a lot like being ignored. Whether others listen at the time is not a measure of what your ideas, or you, are worth.

name: Eunice Newton Foote
setback: In 1856 Eunice Foote showed experimentally that carbon dioxide traps heat. She did not present the work herself; Joseph Henry read it at a scientific meeting, and those who heard of it did not seem to know what to make of it. Her findings faded into obscurity, and credit went for many years to John Tyndall.
after: In 2011 geologist Raymond Sorenson came across an account of her work and published a paper noting her role as a climate pioneer. That set off a wave of renewed recognition of her research.
reflection: Good work can go unnoticed for reasons that have nothing to do with its quality. Being overlooked is not the same as having nothing to offer.

name: Marie Tharp
setback: Working at Lamont, Tharp spotted a rift valley running along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge in sounding profiles. Her colleague Bruce Heezen at first dismissed her reading as girl talk. For about the first 20 years of her career she was not allowed on research cruises, and the first published abstract of the findings did not credit her.
after: Heezen was convinced after about half a year. The rift is now seen as key evidence for moving tectonic plates. Recognition came late in her life: she received numerous awards, and in 1997 the Library of Congress named her one of the four greatest cartographers of the 20th century.
reflection: Seeing something before others are ready to see it can be lonely. The worth of careful work does not depend on who is in the room to approve it.

name: J Harlen Bretz
setback: Bretz argued that the strange landscapes of eastern Washington were carved by enormous Ice Age floods. Many colleagues ridiculed the idea, partly because it sounded like catastrophism, and at a 1927 meeting of the Geological Society of Washington his opponents attacked him. More than four decades passed before the theory gained acceptance.
after: Over the following decades evidence accumulated, and the geologic community eventually accepted catastrophic Ice Age flooding. In 1979 the Geological Society of America awarded Bretz its Penrose Medal, its highest honour, when he was in his late nineties.
reflection: Some ideas take far longer to be heard than a single career seems to allow. Being doubted for a long time is not a measure of how carefully you have looked.

name: Charles David Keeling
setback: Soon after Keeling began measuring carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa, budget cuts nearly shut the observatory and almost ended the programme. The monitoring went in and out of fashion with funding agencies, and in 1964 instruments broke down after funding cuts, leaving a small gap in the record.
after: Keeling pieced together money from a variety of sources to keep the measurements going, and later resisted proposals to move the project to a government agency. The Keeling Curve is now described as one of the most important datasets in earth science, though the record still faces funding threats.
reflection: Long, patient work is often the least glamorous to fund. Struggling to keep a project alive says nothing about whether it matters.

name: Milutin Milanković
setback: When the First World War began, Milanković was taken prisoner and held for six months in the Nezsider internment camp under rough conditions, then interned in Budapest. Working on his orbital theory of the ice ages, he found that scientists did not readily accept it; meteorologists objected that orbital changes were too small to matter.
after: In Budapest he was allowed to work in the library of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences and kept developing his calculations. His ideas were still dismissed into the 1960s, but deep-sea sediment studies and climate models in the late 1960s and 1970s showed his view was correct.
reflection: Work done in hard circumstances still counts, even when the world is slow to agree with it. A cool reception is not a final verdict on your thinking.

name: Inge Lehmann
setback: Lehmann had to accept restrictions in her academic career because of her gender, and worked in a new position with little prestige and plenty of administrative work. Her 1936 evidence for a solid inner core was quickly recognised internationally, but in Denmark it was largely ignored.
after: Her three-layered model of the Earth became generally accepted, and she later received many honours, including an honorary doctorate from Columbia University in 1965; a seismic boundary is named after her. Recognition at home stayed limited: she was never admitted to the Royal Danish Academy.
reflection: Recognition can arrive unevenly, warm in one place and absent in another. Neither tells the whole truth about the value of what you found.

The overlooked genius of geophysics

name: Mary Anning
setback: Anning grew up in poverty in Lyme Regis, collecting and selling fossils. The Geological Society of London refused to admit her because it did not accept women, and many of her finds ended up in museums and collections without credit to her as the discoverer. She was still under financial strain at the end of her life.
after: She was given an annuity some years before her death and became the first honorary member of the Dorset County Museum. Her death was recorded by the Geological Society, and her role in early palaeontology is now widely acknowledged, including a statue unveiled in Lyme Regis in 2022.
reflection: Being shut out of the rooms where credit is handed out does not make a contribution smaller. Your work can matter even when your name is left off it.

Mary Anning (1799-1847)

name: Rachel Carson
setback: Before and after Silent Spring appeared in 1962, Carson faced a relentless attack from the pesticide industry. Producers pressured her publisher, trade journals criticised the book before release, and industry representatives labelled her hysterical, emotional and unscientific.
after: Many scientists agreed with her and public concern grew. President Kennedy appointed a panel to examine her conclusions, and its report supported her case. In 1972 the EPA banned nearly all uses of DDT.
reflection: Being publicly attacked for careful work can be exhausting. Other people trying to discredit you does not change what your evidence shows.

sources.label: Rachel Carson
Rachel Carson

name: Henrietta Swan Leavitt
setback: Leavitt worked as one of the Harvard computers, women who catalogued stars on photographic plates, for 30 cents an hour, within limits on the work women were allowed to do. Her analysis of Cepheid variable stars went largely unacknowledged by her peers, and her death in 1921 drew little attention.
after: A Nobel nomination letter arrived in 1925, after her death, so she never received it. Edwin Hubble later used her period-luminosity relationship to show the Universe is expanding, and it remains one of the best tools for measuring cosmic distances.
reflection: Quiet, careful work can be foundational even when no one says so at the time. Your worth is not set by how loudly your field notices you.

sources.label: Celebrate Henrietta Swan Leavitt's 150th Birthday
Dec. 12, 1921: The death of Henrietta Swan Leavitt

name: Vera Rubin
setback: Rubin could not get into graduate school at Princeton, which did not admit women to its programme at the time. Later, Palomar Observatory officially barred women. When she and Kent Ford published evidence that galaxies hold unseen mass, the findings were initially met with scepticism.
after: She trained at Cornell and Georgetown. In 1965 she became the first woman to observe officially at Palomar. Her work with Ford gradually gained acceptance as some of the first convincing evidence for dark matter, and she received the National Medal of Science, though never a Nobel Prize.
reflection: A closed door says more about the institution than about the person knocking. Scepticism toward new results is normal and does not decide what they are worth.

sources.label: Vera Rubin, dark matter discoverer, dies at 88
Vera Rubin: pioneer of dark matter
Vera Rubin (1928-2016)

name: Beatrice Tinsley
setback: After moving to Dallas, Tinsley found no career opportunities there and was cut off from others in her field, commuting about 300 km each way to Austin for her PhD. Nepotism rules kept her from a permanent post while her husband worked at the university, so she relied on grants and temporary or part-time contracts, and a proposal of hers was turned down.
after: Toward the end of 1974 she accepted an associate professorship at Yale, a permanent post where her work was recognised. In 1978 she was appointed full professor, the first woman professor of astronomy at Yale.
reflection: Rules and circumstances can block a path for reasons that have nothing to do with ability. Needing to go somewhere else to be valued is not a personal failing.

name: Clair Patterson
setback: After Patterson published evidence in 1963 that industrial lead was contaminating the environment, petroleum industry leaders pressured him to stop, threatening to withhold their financial support. The American Petroleum Institute pulled funding for his ocean sediment research and attacked his character.
after: He continued the work with support from government sources. Lead was later removed from residential paint, and leaded gasoline was banned in the United States from 1 January 1996; children's blood lead levels fell sharply as the phase-out went on.
reflection: Losing support because your findings are unwelcome is a real and heavy cost. It reflects the pressure around the work, not a flaw in the person doing it.

sources.label: Immeasurable: Clair C. Patterson
Origins of the 50th Earth Day

name: Shuji Nakamura
setback: While working on blue LEDs at the Japanese company Nichia, Nakamura went years without results. His boss lost interest, a request for equipment was refused for lack of budget, and colleagues felt he was wasting company money. A later company president ordered him to stop the gallium nitride work.
after: He kept working on gallium nitride. He later moved to the University of California, Santa Barbara, in 2000, and shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.
reflection: Being seen as a cost by the people around you says nothing about what you are worth. Their impatience was about their own timelines, not about you.

sources.label: Shuji Nakamura – Biographical
Let there be light

name: Isamu Akasaki
setback: Growing gallium nitride crystals for blue LEDs was widely seen as extremely difficult, and many researchers abandoned the approach. Earlier, at Matsushita, management decided to stop blue LED research, and some of his own group members objected to his choice of method. He described his path as going alone into the wilderness.
after: At Nagoya University from 1981, his group developed ways to grow high-quality gallium nitride crystals. The field later grew into a large research area, and he shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.
reflection: Working on something most others have set aside can feel lonely. That loneliness is a circumstance, not a verdict on your judgement or your worth.

sources.label: Isamu Akasaki (obituary)
Isamu Akasaki – blue LED research

name: Hiroshi Amano
setback: As a student at Nagoya University, Amano spent years trying and failing to grow high-quality gallium nitride crystals. Near the end of his master course he described himself as still carrying out lonely, fruitless experiments, working in a makeshift lab.
after: In 1985 he succeeded in growing gallium nitride with an atomically flat surface. Work on other problems, such as p-type doping, took several more years. He later shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.
reflection: Long stretches of experiments that do not work are a normal part of research. They are not a measure of how capable or valuable you are.

sources.label: Hiroshi Amano – Biographical
Nobel winner Hiroshi Amano tells of hard road, bright future
sources.publisher: Yale School of Engineering & Applied Science

name: Yitang Zhang
setback: After finishing his mathematics PhD in 1991, Zhang could not find academic work. For several years he worked outside academia, including as an accountant and at a Subway sandwich shop, before taking a lecturer post at the University of New Hampshire.
after: In 2013, in his late fifties, he submitted a proof that there are infinitely many pairs of primes separated by less than 70 million. Referees confirmed it within weeks as a landmark result.
reflection: Years spent outside the usual academic path do not erase your mind or your love of a subject. Where you work is not the same as who you are.

sources.label: After Prime Proof, an Unlikely Star Rises
Yitang Zhang's Spectacular Mathematical Journey

name: Srinivasa Ramanujan
setback: Ramanujan passed mathematics but failed his other subjects, lost his scholarship and could not continue at university. Working as a clerk in Madras, he sent his results to the Cambridge mathematicians E. W. Hobson and H. F. Baker, but neither replied.
after: In 1913 he wrote to G. H. Hardy, who replied with great interest. The University of Madras granted him a scholarship, and in 1914 he went to Trinity College, Cambridge, beginning a celebrated collaboration with Hardy.
reflection: Silence from the people you hoped would notice your work is painful, but it is not a judgement of your ability. Exam results and unanswered letters are only part of the story.

name: Aziz Sancar
setback: Sancar, who grew up in Turkey, felt unprepared and isolated during an early stay at Johns Hopkins University in the US and returned home to regroup. Later, during repeated lab failures, a labmate told him he lacked talent for research. He applied to about 50 universities for faculty jobs; by his account, all but one turned him down, some without a reply.
after: The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill offered him a position, the one place that did. He built his career there and shared the 2015 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
reflection: A pile of rejections and one harsh comment from a colleague are not an assessment of your talent. They describe a moment, not a person.

name: Bernardo Houssay
setback: In 1943, after he publicly called for effective democracy in Argentina, the military government removed Houssay from his university chair for political reasons.
after: He declined invitations from abroad and stayed in Argentina, organising a privately funded Institute of Biology and Experimental Medicine. He received the 1947 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and a new government reinstated him at the university in 1955.
reflection: Losing a position for reasons that have nothing to do with your work can shake anyone. It does not reduce the value of what you have built or who you are.

name: June Huh
setback: A bad test score in elementary school convinced Huh he was not good at math. He dropped out of high school at 16 to write poetry and only turned to mathematics in his sixth year of university. Because of his undistinguished undergraduate record, all but one of the graduate programs he applied to rejected him.
after: He began a PhD at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, the one school that accepted him. In 2022 he was awarded the Fields Medal for work connecting geometry and combinatorics.
reflection: An early belief that you are bad at something, or a late start, does not have to settle the question for good. Your path does not need to look like anyone else to count.

name: Mario Molina
setback: Molina, who trained in Mexico, was a postdoc in the lab of F. Sherwood Rowland at the University of California, Irvine, when they published the 1974 finding that CFCs could destroy the ozone layer. The work was initially disputed by industry and met fierce resistance from companies whose businesses relied on CFCs.
after: A National Academy of Sciences review in 1976 supported the work, and the Antarctic ozone hole was reported in 1985. The Montreal Protocol to phase out CFCs followed, and Molina shared the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
reflection: Being disputed by powerful voices is hard, especially early in a career. Resistance to your findings is not the same as a judgement of your integrity or worth.

Mario Molina, Nobel laureate who revealed threat to ozone layer, dies at 77

name: Luis F. Leloir
setback: Leloir did his research in Buenos Aires at a privately funded institute. His laboratory had meager financial resources and lacked new equipment, and much of the work was done with limited resources.
after: His team studied how sugars such as lactose are formed and broken down in the body. He received the 1970 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
reflection: Doing research without the equipment or funding others take for granted is a real burden. The limits of your lab are not limits on your worth.

name: Tebello Nyokong
setback: Nyokong was sent to herd sheep as a child and at first chose the arts stream at school because peers called science subjects too difficult. Later, after joining Rhodes University in 1992, she described the early years as very challenging and said she felt academic loneliness, with no one to share ideas with.
after: She went on to lead a team at Rhodes developing cancer treatments based on dyes and light, became the first South African scientist to win the UNESCO-partnered Awards for Women in Science, and received a National Research Foundation Lifetime Achiever Award.
reflection: Feeling intellectually alone in a place is about the place, not about you. Many people carry that isolation quietly, and it says nothing about whether they belong.

sources.label: An outlier redesigns chemistry

name: Emmy Noether
setback: At Göttingen, Noether was not allowed to lecture on her own account, so her courses were advertised under the name of David Hilbert. She worked as an unpaid lecturer and lived in poverty for years; sources say she only began earning a salary in 1923. In 1933 she was dismissed from the university under the Nazi regime because she was Jewish.
after: She took up a visiting professorship at Bryn Mawr College in the USA, funded with Rockefeller Foundation help, and also lectured at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. She died unexpectedly in 1935 after an operation.
reflection: Years without a title or a salary said nothing about the quality of her thinking. Your worth is not measured by the position an institution is willing to give you.

Emmy Noether

name: Gerty Cori
setback: When she moved to Washington University in St. Louis with her husband and research partner Carl Cori, university rules barred appointing two members of the same family to the faculty. She was hired as a research fellow at a token salary of about one tenth of what her husband earned.
after: She was promoted to professor of biological chemistry in July 1947, only months before she shared the 1947 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
reflection: Being placed in a lower rank than your work deserves is a statement about the rules, not about you. Her contribution was real long before her title caught up.

name: Maria Goeppert Mayer
setback: Because of anti-nepotism rules, the universities where her husband worked, including Johns Hopkins and Columbia, did not give her a salary or a full-time post. She spent many years in unpaid positions; at Columbia she had office space but no salary, and she later taught classes for which she was not paid.
after: She developed the nuclear shell model and shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physics. She was 58 before she became a full professor, at the University of California, San Diego, in 1960.
reflection: Doing serious work without pay or status does not make the work any less yours. Recognition can arrive very late, and a person is valuable long before it does.

name: Ada Yonath
setback: When she set out to determine the structure of the ribosome by crystallography, many scientists reacted with disbelief and even ridicule. Some predicted the project was a dead end, and she has said she was seen for years as the village fool.
after: The effort took more than two decades. The first complete structures of both bacterial ribosomal subunits were published in 2000 and 2001, and she shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
reflection: Being doubted by respected colleagues is painful, and it does not mean you are foolish for trying. Your worth does not depend on whether others believe in your project.

name: Nettie Stevens
setback: Stevens only began working as a research scientist at age 39. After she concluded that chromosomes determine sex, most scientists did not accept her theory immediately, and many textbooks gave sole credit to Edmund Wilson, who reached a similar result around the same time. At Bryn Mawr she held the modest post of associate in experimental morphology.
after: The next 11 years were the most productive of her life. She died of breast cancer in 1912, and her role in discovering how sex is determined by chromosomes is now widely acknowledged.
reflection: Starting late and being overlooked does not shrink what you contribute. The value of careful work does not depend on who is credited at the time.

name: Marie Curie
setback: In January 1911, Curie stood for the single vacant physics seat in the French Academy of Sciences. She lost the election to Édouard Branly by two votes, and she never became a member of the Academy.
after: Eleven months later she was named the sole recipient of the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The first woman elected to the Academy was her former student Marguerite Perey, in 1962.
reflection: Even someone already celebrated can be turned away by an institution. A rejection like this reflects the room you were in, not the measure of your work.

The day Marie Curie got snubbed by the French science world

name: Williamina Fleming
setback: Fleming first came to the Harvard College Observatory world as a maid in the home of its director, Edward Pickering. Women computers there earned a base wage far below entry-level men; in 1900 her own hourly pay was about one fifth of what male assistants earned, and she recorded in her journal being told her salary was excellent for a woman.
after: In 1899 she was named Curator of Astronomical Photographs, the first Harvard Corporation appointment of a woman. She discovered 10 novae, 59 gaseous nebulae and more than 300 variable stars.
reflection: Where you start, and what you are paid, does not decide what you can see or understand. Unfair treatment is worth naming, and it is never a verdict on your worth.

Brief life of Williamina Fleming

name: Mary Jackson
setback: Jackson joined the segregated West Area Computing section at Langley in 1951. To take the courses needed for promotion to engineer, she needed special permission from the City of Hampton to sit in class with white students. Later, as an engineer, she was unable to break into management-level grades.
after: In 1958 she became the first Black female engineer at NASA. In 1979 she left engineering, accepting a lower grade to become Langley Federal Women's Program Manager, working to widen opportunities for women and minorities.
reflection: Hitting a ceiling built by others is not a personal failing. Choosing a different path can be a thoughtful decision, not a defeat.

sources.label: Mary W. Jackson biography
Mary W. Jackson

name: Dorothy Vaughan
setback: Vaughan was assigned to the segregated West Area Computing unit at Langley, whose members were at first required to use separate dining and bathroom facilities. After segregated facilities were abolished in 1958, she sought another management position at Langley but never received one.
after: In 1949 she had become the first Black supervisor at NACA, leading the West Computers. After 1958 she joined the new Analysis and Computation Division, became an expert FORTRAN programmer, contributed to the Scout launch vehicle program, and retired from NASA in 1971.
reflection: Being passed over does not erase what you have built or the people you have helped. A career can hold real achievement and real unfairness at the same time.

sources.label: Dorothy Vaughan

name: Esther Lederberg
setback: Lederberg discovered the lambda bacteriophage and, with Joshua Lederberg, developed replica plating. When Joshua and two others received the 1958 Nobel Prize, she was not among them. To obtain her post at Stanford medical school, she offered to start in an untenured slot even though she felt overqualified.
after: She served as a professor of medical microbiology at Stanford, directed the Plasmid Reference Center from 1976 to the mid-1980s, and was professor emerita at her death in 2006. Colleagues describe her lambda discovery as highly influential.
reflection: Quiet or uncredited work can still be foundational. Your contribution matters even when the spotlight falls elsewhere.

name: Douglas Prasher
setback: In the 1990s at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in Massachusetts, Douglas Prasher isolated the gene for green fluorescent protein and freely shared it with other researchers. His funding proposals to the US National Institutes of Health were turned down, and he eventually left science. By 2008 he was driving a courtesy shuttle for a car dealership in Alabama.
after: When the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognised work on this protein, laureates Martin Chalfie and Roger Tsien, who had both received the gene from him, invited Prasher and his wife to the ceremony in Stockholm. Some years later he returned to research as a staff research associate in the Tsien lab, working on fluorescent proteins again.
reflection: A career can stall for reasons that say nothing about the quality of your work. What you contributed stays real, even in seasons when no one is funding it.

name: Rainer Weiss
setback: Rainer Weiss wrote down his idea for a laser interferometer to detect gravitational waves at MIT in 1972. Turning it into LIGO took decades of stops and starts in research and funding. Many in the scientific community thought the project was too complicated to build, and it was in trouble in the early 1990s.
after: With backing from the US National Science Foundation, the detectors were built and then needed years of fine-tuning. On 14 September 2015, more than four decades after the original idea, LIGO detected gravitational waves from two merging black holes. Weiss shared the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics.
reflection: Some questions take far longer than one project or one grant. The worth of your work is not measured by how quickly it pays off.

MIT physicist Rainer Weiss shares Nobel Prize in Physics

name: Geoffrey Hinton
setback: For many years Hinton worked on artificial neural networks while most people in artificial intelligence said they would never work.
after: At the University of Toronto, Hinton and his students improved neural networks for recognising objects in images, cutting error rates roughly in half. He shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics.
reflection: Working on an idea that others dismiss can feel lonely. Their doubt is not a verdict on your judgement or your worth.

Former CMU faculty Geoffrey Hinton awarded 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics

name: John B. Goodenough
setback: In the mid-1980s, John Goodenough realised he would lose his job at the University of Oxford once he reached the university retirement age.
after: He moved to the University of Texas at Austin, starting there in 1986 at the age of 64. He led research in his field for more than three decades afterwards and still came to his lab daily well into his late 90s.
reflection: Institutional rules can close a door that has nothing to do with your ability. A forced move is a hard thing, and it does not erase what you still have to offer.

name: Michael Houghton
setback: After joining Chiron Corporation in California in 1982, Michael Houghton devoted his lab to finding the cause of non-A, non-B hepatitis. For years he and colleagues tried many approaches without success. He later recalled that after two or three years they still had nothing, because their methods were not sensitive enough.
after: After a key discussion in 1985, the team tried an immunoscreening approach and changed the patient serum they used. In 1989 Houghton and collaborators published the discovery of the hepatitis C virus genome, about seven years after starting. He shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
reflection: Years of experiments that do not work can make you question yourself. Those years are still real work, whatever the outcome turns out to be.

name: Frances Arnold
setback: In 2019 Frances Arnold and colleagues published a paper in Science on the enzymatic synthesis of beta-lactams. Her lab later could not reproduce the results, and key data were missing from a coauthor lab notebook. Arnold said she had been busy when the paper was submitted, in the middle of the Nobel Prize attention, and had not done her job well.
after: In January 2020 she announced the retraction publicly and apologised; all three coauthors agreed to it and also apologised. Chemistry World described her apology as simple and direct, explaining without making excuses.
reflection: Even the most accomplished researchers get things wrong. Owning a mistake openly is part of doing science well, not a mark against who you are.

name: Pamela Ronald
setback: Pamela Ronald and her UC Davis lab had reported that a bacterial protein called Ax21 triggers an immune receptor in rice. In 2013, researchers repeating the experiments found a mislabelled bacterial strain and a highly variable test. The lab retracted two papers, from 2009 and 2011, in PLOS One and Science. The university described the errors as unintentional.
after: Ronald announced the errors at an international meeting and corrected the record. Her lab kept working on the question and in 2015 reported in Science Advances the discovery of RaxX, a small bacterial protein recognised by rice plants that carry the immune receptor.
reflection: Finding an error in your own published work is painful. Correcting it honestly is part of good science, and it does not cancel your worth as a researcher.

name: Julia Strand
setback: As an assistant professor of psychology at Carleton College, Julia Strand found that her team could not replicate one of her published results. She then discovered a small programming error in the timing of the original study that invalidated the effect. She described feeling physically ill and briefly considering not telling anyone.
after: She informed her coauthors, the journal, her funder, her department and a student who had used the data, and wrote about the mistake publicly. The journal, Psychonomic Bulletin and Review, added an error notice and published a corrected version instead of retracting the paper. Many researchers responded with support.
reflection: A bug in your code is not a flaw in your character. Telling the truth about it takes courage, and many colleagues will meet that with kindness.

What If I Didn't Tell?

name: Arthur Ashkin
setback: At Bell Labs in 1970, an internal review said a paper by Arthur Ashkin on pushing tiny particles with light was not suitable for Physical Review Letters. Later, after difficulties with trapping atoms, Bell Labs leadership soured on his atom-trapping experiments and pushed him toward other work.
after: His boss told him to submit the 1970 paper anyway, and it was accepted immediately. Ashkin later trapped tiny particles with a single laser beam and worked with Steven Chu on cooling and trapping atoms. At age 96 he shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics for optical trapping.
reflection: Internal reviews and managers do not always see the value in an idea straight away. Their hesitation is not a measure of what you are capable of.

Colder: how physicists beat the theoretical limit for laser cooling

name: Thomas C. Südhof
setback: In the mid-1990s Thomas Südhof was recruited to set up a neuroscience department at the Max Planck Institute in Göttingen, commuting from the US. A new institute president had doubts about the recruitment, wanted a different direction and suggested he resign. Südhof later said he was young and not confident enough, so he looked for a new job.
after: He resigned and returned to the United States, where he continued his research on synapses. Some questions he had worked on for decades were only answered by his lab many years later. He shared the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
reflection: A position can fall apart because of people and politics rather than your science. Leaving a role that does not work is not the same as failing.
