Nobel laureate Südhof on leaving Göttingen

name: Minakshi Poddar
setback: Halfway through her PhD in molecular biology and biochemistry at Wesleyan University, her husband moved to Pittsburgh for work. She tried a long-distance arrangement for a while, then left the PhD to join him. She called it a big decision.
after: She completed the requirements for a masters degree instead. She later became a senior lab coordinator at the University of Pittsburgh, and the article says she is fully satisfied with her career choices.
reflection: Leaving a programme for the sake of your life outside the lab is a real choice, not a lesser one. A finished degree is not the only measure of a good path.

sources.label: To quit or not?

name: Lois Wardell
setback: After a postdoc at McGill University, she took an industry job in Tucson managing unmanned aircraft development. New hurdles to getting permission to fly unmanned aircraft hit the company, and she was laid off.
after: She said she had loved the job but missed research, so she tried to move back into academia. She attended a workshop for people returning to academic careers and was interviewing for jobs. She found interviews hard to get but had received positive feedback and felt optimistic. The article does not say how the search ended.
reflection: Losing a job because of rules outside your control says nothing about your ability. Careers can loop back as well as move forward.

sources.label: Managing change: Returning to academia

name: Kim Nilsson
setback: Doubts about an academic career began during her astrophysics PhD, and she found she most enjoyed the project-management side of research. After two more postdocs, she spent about a year applying for jobs outside academia and was unsuccessful in all of those applications.
after: She then did an MBA. Afterwards she met her co-founder and set up Pivigo, a company that trains researchers moving into data science.
reflection: A year of unanswered applications reflects a hard transition, not a lack of worth. Sometimes skills simply need a new setting to be seen.

sources.label: Working Scientist podcast: Career transitions from physics to data science

name: Lewis Armitage
setback: He worked on the ATLAS experiment, partly based at CERN, and decided to leave because he wanted his weekends back. In his job search he found it hard to present his skills, and his many applications mostly came back negative, even after he reworked his CV and cover letters.
after: Finding a job took a little less than a year. He became a data analyst at a consumer-behaviour consultancy in Geneva.
reflection: Wanting a life outside work is a reasonable reason to change course. A slow job search is common and is not a verdict on you.

sources.label: Working Scientist podcast: Career transitions from physics to data science

name: Elizabeth Tasker
setback: As a foreign faculty member at Hokkaido University, the details of her research award were given to her in Japanese. She missed small print saying the funding would end once she was tenured, which left her with only about eighteen months of it. She said she was very upset and came close to leaving.
after: The postdocs she had hired still came, and the university international support office took over her grant management. She passed her tenure review, became an associate professor, and later moved to JAXA.
reflection: Working in a second language means some things will be missed, and that is not carelessness. Asking for help with it is part of the job.

sources.label: Working Scientist podcast: Global career moves, and how to survive them

name: Mariana Viglino
setback: After a PhD and a postdoc, she won a permanent research position at CONICET in Patagonia, studying fossil dolphins. Then Argentine science funding was cut. She described working in survival mode, barely publishing the required articles, and having to put her plans for building a research group on hold.
after: At the time of the interview she had just started a three-month placement in Germany. She said being able to focus on science there had already changed her mood and brought back her creativity. Her longer-term plans were not settled.
reflection: When the ground shifts under a whole research system, a stalled plan is not a personal shortcoming. Getting through a hard stretch also counts.

sources.label: How to pause and restart your science career (Nature Careers podcast)

name: Gabriela Lopez
setback: As an Afro-Latinx first-generation college graduate, she had no family members who could tell her what a PhD would be like. She struggled with first-year classes and spent many hours in tutoring. She was then told she had failed her qualifying exam on her third attempt, which meant dismissal from the programme.
after: When her essay was republished in 2022, she was described as a PhD candidate at Northwestern University, and she wrote that her story has a happy ending.
reflection: One exam measures one hour, not a person. Not having a map of academia is a real disadvantage, not a lack of ability.

sources.label: My Ph.D. qualifying exam was a nightmare, but I am not letting it define me
Republished essay

name: Cheryl Dembe
setback: In 1971 she was one of very few women in the University of Chicago chemistry department. Her adviser died suddenly, and she was told her only option was to start over on a new project with a new adviser. Seeing no way to finish, she left for California.
after: She taught chemistry, including 34 years at Diablo Valley College, retiring in 2008. In 2018 she wrote to the university president asking about her degree. A committee reviewed her notebooks and data and awarded her the PhD, and she joined the 2019 graduation ceremony.
reflection: Work does not stop being valuable because circumstances blocked it from being recognised. A long gap does not erase what was done.

sources.label: 50 years after sexism forced her out of chemistry, Cheryl Dembe is graduating

name: Ellen Kirkpatrick
setback: After her doctorate she applied for every fellowship and job she could, and rejections for early-career posts piled up. She could rarely relocate for short, poorly paid contracts, gave up conferences and memberships she could not afford, and lost library access when her university ties ended.
after: About a year and a half after her viva, she was working as an independent scholar with a book forthcoming. She wrote openly that she was no longer sure she wanted to remain an academic.
reflection: Not knowing what comes next is an honest place to be, not a failure. Questioning a system is different from failing in it.

sources.label: The academy I dreamed of for 20 years no longer exists, and I am waking up

name: Nazima Kadir
setback: After a Yale PhD she lacked the publications and connections for a full-time academic post. The teaching work she found paid about 100 pounds a week. Her book was shortlisted for an ethnography award, then taken off the shortlist, she reports, because she did not have an academic job.
after: She moved to the private sector and works as an applied anthropologist in design, innovation and branding, creating people-centred products and services for clients. She wrote that she was glad she chose this path.
reflection: Your work does not lose its value because it lacks an institutional label. Skills from research can find a home in many places.

sources.label: I am glad I eschewed a career in academia

name: Marina Kovačević
setback: She began her chemistry PhD at the University of Novi Sad with no funding and took bartending and waitressing jobs to get by. Two years in, she switched from medicinal chemistry to computational chemistry when a funded position opened in another lab, overhauling her research focus.
after: When Nature profiled her in 2019, she was a third-year PhD student working long hours. The article described her future as uncertain.
reflection: Working side jobs to keep going is a sign of commitment, not of falling behind. Starting over in a new area takes courage.

sources.label: PhDs: the tortuous truth

name: Miyo K. Chatanaka
setback: Three years into her PhD at the University of Toronto on Alzheimer disease biomarkers, she had no publications, no usable data and no conference presentations, and the methods had proven unreliable. She told her supervisor she saw no way forward without another four years just to make the project work.
after: Her supervisor and a committee member suggested starting a new project, and she switched to glioma biomarkers. About two years later she had presented at three international conferences and published her second research paper.
reflection: Years without results often reflect a hard problem, not a weak researcher. Changing direction is a decision, not a defeat.

sources.label: How I started my Ph.D. research over after 3 years

name: Emily M. Bartholomay
setback: During her PhD at Southern Illinois University Carbondale, her advisor announced to the lab that she would be leaving the university in just over a year. She wrote that she was shocked, angry and worried about what it would mean for her studies.
after: She reviewed the research interests of faculty in her department and joined a different lab there. Within a year of starting in the new lab, she successfully proposed her dissertation.
reflection: Losing a supervisor is a disruption you did not cause. Feeling shaken by it is normal, and finding a new footing takes time.

sources.label: The hard task of switching supervisors during graduate studies

name: Natalie James
setback: About two and a half years into a funded chemistry PhD at the University of Warwick, she left the programme during what she described as a very bad time in her life. She was offered time off or the option of writing up for a masters degree, and chose neither.
after: With help from the university counselling service, she came to see the PhD as the wrong choice for her in the first place. She went on to work in administration at Warwick.
reflection: Stepping away from something that is harming you can be a sound decision. A degree left unfinished does not cancel the person who started it.

sources.label: The PhD experience: this far, and no further

name: Devoney Looser
setback: Looser estimated she received roughly 1,000 rejections over two decades, about one a week. That included nearly 400 teaching jobs and postdoctoral fellowships, a first book proposal turned down six times, and an edited collection rejected 12 times at the proposal stage.
after: She stayed in academia and became a professor of English at Arizona State University. She wrote that she now sees rejection as part of every stage of an academic career, and she urged senior scholars to make their own shadow CVs public.
reflection: A long list of no answers is a record of how often you tried. It says little about what you are worth.

sources.label: Me and My Shadow CV
ASU Piper Center announces recipient of 2017 faculty fellowship

name: Bradley Voytek
setback: As an undergraduate at USC, Voytek failed a class in his first quarter, lost his scholarships and was placed on academic probation. With a GPA below 3.0 he received only one PhD offer, and he said he struggled to publish for years, trying and failing again and again.
after: He switched from physics to psychology, graduated, did his PhD at UC Berkeley and became an assistant professor at UC San Diego. He lists rejections and failures on his CV, and says he values skills and motivation over grades when choosing lab members.
reflection: A rough start shows where you were at one moment, not what you are capable of. Grades and rejections are only a small part of a person.

sources.label: Scientists, advertise your failures

name: Mitch Brown
setback: While preparing a follow-up study, Brown found a coding error in his own 2021 paper: values for two targets had been reversed. Once recalculated, one of the main findings was no longer supported by the data. He described the experience as terrifying.
after: He and his co-authors asked for the paper to be retracted and planned to submit a corrected version. He said his colleagues never wavered in supporting his decision, and that he wanted to do his part to keep science self-correcting.
reflection: Finding your own mistake can feel frightening. Correcting it openly is part of careful work, not a mark against you.

sources.label: A terrifying experience: A team of researchers does the right thing when they find an error

name: Daniel Bolnick
setback: In 2016 a colleague could not reproduce the data from Bolnick's 2009 paper. He found he had misused a statistical tool in R, and the error negated his findings. He said it felt horrid, with a sinking feeling in his gut and a hard time sleeping that night.
after: He contacted the journal right away to request a retraction and wrote a detailed public post explaining the mistake. He said sending in the retraction hurt his pride. Many readers responded with support.
reflection: An honest error is something that happens to careful people too. How you respond to it can matter more than the error itself.

sources.label: A sinking feeling in my gut: Diary of a retraction

name: Hermann Grassmann
setback: Grassmann's major mathematical book was far ahead of its time and was largely ignored. When he applied for a university post, a report by the mathematician Kummer described the work as good material in a deficient form, which ended his hopes of a university position.
after: Disappointed that he could not convince mathematicians, he turned to linguistics, studying Sanskrit and Gothic. In his lifetime he gained more recognition for languages, including election to the American Oriental Society. His mathematical methods were adopted only slowly, later inspiring the work of Élie Cartan.
reflection: Being overlooked by the people around you does not settle the value of your ideas. Some work simply meets its readers late.

sources.label: Hermann Grassmann biography
sources.publisher: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews

name: James T. Dakin
setback: After a PhD in experimental high-energy physics at Princeton and a postdoc at Stanford, Dakin was an assistant professor at UMass Amherst. Around age 30 he felt locked into his specialty, worried about its future, and found the theory behind his experiments had moved beyond his comprehension.
after: He left academia for the GE Research and Development Center and spent 37 years at GE, mostly in lighting technology, later working on LEDs, then ran a consulting business. He wrote that he never regretted the decision but will never know where the other path might have led.
reflection: Leaving a path you trained for can be a considered choice rather than a defeat. Not knowing what the other road held is part of any choice.

sources.label: A physicist out of academia (letter)

name: Russell D'Souza
setback: D'Souza's first PhD project at Wayne State, on a little-studied protein variant, stalled. He got through only two of ten planned variants, spent almost a year without solid data, and by the end of his third year had little to show. He was almost ready to quit.
after: With his mentor and committee he switched to a smaller project in the same yeast system and found features not reported before. He graduated in 2016 and later became a postdoctoral fellow at the NIH. He wonders if switching earlier would have saved a year, but says he has no regrets.
reflection: A project that stalls is not proof that you cannot do research. Sometimes the problem is the project, not the person.

sources.label: Project swap

name: Guzal Khayrullina
setback: During about four and a half years of PhD work at the Uniformed Services University, Khayrullina described hundreds of failed experiments behind each small piece of data, along with equipment problems and disruption from the pandemic.
after: She completed her neuroscience PhD and moved on to a postdoctoral fellowship at the National Institutes of Health in neuro-oncology research.
reflection: Most experiments do not work, and that is true for everyone. The ones that fail are part of the work, not a verdict on you.

sources.label: Persistence, Resilience and Fortitude are Hallmarks of USU Neuroscience Graduate

name: Suzanne Shu
setback: Shu failed her first dissertation defense. She says her advisors had been largely hands-off, so she had little feedback beforehand, and the criticism at the defense was harsh.
after: Her advisor gave her a chance to revise. She spent a summer on the research while her mother cared for her children, reframed the dissertation as a roadmap, and later turned it into several publications. She became a marketing professor and a dean at Cornell.
reflection: Failing an exam or defense is an event, not an identity. Many people who did go on to teach others once stood exactly there.

sources.label: Faculty Who Failed Series: Suzanne Shu

name: Avery August
setback: At the end of his third year of graduate school, August had to change advisors and labs and start a new project, with no formal results from his first three years. He considered leaving.
after: He decided to continue, partly because he did not want to disappoint his family, and completed his PhD. He says the first three years taught him how to do science, which helped the new project start faster. He later became a professor of immunology and deputy provost at Cornell.
reflection: Starting over can feel like losing years. What you learned in that time usually stays with you, even when it does not show on paper.

sources.label: Faculty Who Failed Series: Avery August

name: Kathryn J. Boor
setback: As a graduate student at the University of Wisconsin, Boor felt her failed lab experiments showed she was not cut out for science. Believing she had to solve problems alone, she abruptly withdrew from graduate school without discussing it with her advisor.
after: She later reconnected with her advisor, who worked with her on a project with smallholder farms in Kenya. After two years she completed a master's thesis there, an experience she says redirected her career. She later became dean of Cornell's Graduate School.
reflection: Stepping away does not erase what you can do. Asking for help can feel hard, and it is never a sign that you do not belong.

sources.label: Faculty Who Failed Series: Kathryn J. Boor

name: David Bindel
setback: During his PhD at Berkeley, Bindel failed a three-hour oral preliminary exam in numerical methods. He says he was incoherent by the end, and one examiner told him he had not shown he knew anything. He was crushed and considered leaving.
after: His advisor wrote to explain the examiners wanted recall, not derivation, and helped him list material to learn. He passed on the retake the next semester and became a professor of computer science at Cornell. He says that to fail is not the same as being a failure.
reflection: One bad exam measures one afternoon. You are more than any single result, real or perceived.

sources.label: Faculty Who Failed Series: David Bindel

name: Kelly (Jun) Liu
setback: Early in her thesis research, Liu could not get her PCR to work, and when it did she did not get enough DNA for later experiments. Seeing classmates advance faster, she felt disappointed in her progress and began to doubt her ability to do science.
after: She realised she had been repeating experiments without thinking more deeply, sought advice inside and outside her lab, and improved her troubleshooting. A side project from her advisor helped her regain confidence. She later became a professor at Cornell.
reflection: Comparing your pace with others can make normal struggles feel personal. You are not defined only by the low points.

sources.label: Faculty Who Failed Series: Kelly Liu

name: Vetjaera Haakuria
setback: At the University of Namibia, Haakuria wanted to test whether bacteria in termite mounds make chemicals that kill microbes, but his lab lacked the equipment to do the work. He said there was no way to carry out the research without it.
after: In 2016 the nonprofit Seeding Labs sent instruments including a sonicator and water baths. His team then collected termite-mound soil and began the analysis.
reflection: Being held back by missing tools is not a shortcoming in you. Circumstances shape what is possible, sometimes for a long time.

sources.label: Science on a shoestring

name: Abdoulaye Djimdé
setback: Working in Mali, Djimdé described waiting months for reagents: a test that could begin within days in the United States could take three months to set up in Bamako.
after: He continued his research and received funding to train African scientists in bioinformatics, hoping they would not need to seek help from Europe or America.
reflection: Slow progress caused by distance and supply delays says nothing about ability. Working within hard limits is its own kind of skill.

sources.label: Science on a shoestring

name: Lotteke Swier
setback: Swier, a PhD candidate in Groningen, had almost three years of research on a transport protein when another group published a study of the same protein in 2015. She said she became withdrawn for a while, and her supervisor recalled that tears were shed.
after: She and her supervisor reanalysed her data. Their paper was published in Nature Communications, showing the protein's inner workings in motion rather than as a single snapshot.
reflection: Being scooped can feel like losing years of effort. The work and skill you built are still yours.

sources.label: Beaten to the punch

name: Clarisa Medina
setback: Clarisa Medina failed her doctoral qualifying exam, a 36 hour test, in summer 2023 and again that December. Two failures meant dismissal, and the program director told her that her time in the program was over. It came during a year in which she also lost her grandfather.
after: She appealed in April 2024 and, after thirty days of waiting, was allowed a third attempt alongside the cohort below her. She passed in July 2024 and writes that she is now working on her dissertation.
reflection: She writes that she did not fail because she was not smart enough, but because life at that point was overwhelming.

sources.label: The Year That Tried to Break Me: A PhD Survival Story
sources.publisher: Boston University, Emerging World Leaders, April 2025

name: Brittany Trang
setback: The first half of Brittany Trang's chemistry PhD at Northwestern University was a run of disappointing or inexplicable results. By her own count, her dissertation held two years of work with inconsistent results and eight failed projects. A method she developed worked until it did not.
after: A later project, on a possible way to destroy PFAS chemicals, was published in Science a few months before she wrote the essay. She earned her PhD in 2022 and was then a science reporting fellow at STAT News.
reflection: When she cleared out her lab bench she found a thick stack of notes from everything that had not worked, and could not bring herself to throw it out. Those years were still part of her training, even though no paper shows them.

sources.label: STEM graduate programs should embrace failure
sources.publisher: ASBMB Today, December 2022 (first published by Undark)

name: Hanna Erickson
setback: Hanna Erickson joined a small immunotherapy lab and designed her project from scratch, in an area neither of her mentors knew well. After eight months it had barely started. Days before she was due to submit a fellowship application, one mentor told her the proposal was not ready and the project would not suit a timely PhD.
after: About a year into the program she switched to a lab studying liver biology and liver cancer. She writes that her first advisor was receptive and that she left on good terms. Her author note lists her as an MD-PhD candidate at the University of Illinois.
reflection: A year can feel like too much to walk away from. She weighed it against the years still ahead and moved.

sources.label: Why I switched thesis labs in graduate school
sources.publisher: Editage Insights, March 2019 (first published on the author's blog, 2014)

name: Kellie Vinal
setback: In her second year, Kellie Vinal had a panic attack in the middle of her oral qualifying exam and could not recall even basic facts. The committee failed her and advised her to leave with a master's degree. She later heard that her adviser wanted her out of the lab.
after: She started therapy and learned she had generalized anxiety disorder and depression. Over the summer she met many professors and found one willing to take her on. She wrote a new proposal and passed her second qualifying exam.
reflection: The exam measured one very bad day. With therapy and a different lab, the second attempt went differently.

sources.label: Kellie Vinal: This Big, Significant Moment of Truth

name: Connacher Murphy
setback: Connacher Murphy started an economics PhD in 2022 and writes that he was miserable. He began taking an antidepressant after his first year and grew lonelier in his second. He also tried and failed to publish a paper from his earlier research job, and came to doubt that he was suited to academic life.
after: He left the program by mid 2024 for a full-time job at a think tank where he had been working part time. He writes that the move was not better in every way. He gave up research freedom and expects some regret when his friends finish.
reflection: He does not tell it as a clean win. Leaving gave him some things and cost him others, and he says so.

sources.label: Quitting: Why I left my PhD program

name: Simon Spichak
setback: Simon Spichak's PhD at University College Cork depended on growing a type of brain cell called microglia in a dish, and most of his experiments went wrong. In a lab of more than 40 people he had little supervision, and he developed mental health problems. He estimated that finishing would take at least two more years.
after: He switched projects, focused on bioinformatics and left with a master's degree. He moved home to Toronto, became a freelance science journalist and founded a company that helps students get low-cost therapy. He says leaving felt like failure at first, and that the feeling lifted after about a week.
reflection: He decided his health mattered more to him than the diploma. Leaving with a master's was his own choice.

sources.label: 4 PhD students (besides me) who “Mastered out” and became science writers

name: Chelsea Corkins
setback: Chelsea Corkins began a PhD at Virginia Tech in 2013 and did well in many ways, but doubts crept in. She was not enthralled with research and looked forward to teaching instead. She has said that without her mentors she might have walked away with no degree at all.
after: With support from her dean she took time off to work in an agricultural education program, then enrolled in a different master's program. She graduated in 2019, six years after arriving, and took a community engagement job in agricultural extension at the University of Missouri.
reflection: She prefers the word pivot to mastering out. The article reports that she does not regret leaving the PhD.

sources.label: Mastering Out

name: Jessica Ernakovich
setback: The first experiment of Jessica Ernakovich's PhD ended with some of her soil samples in the trash when the lab freezer was cleaned out. She writes that she had started without a clear question, so she did not know what to analyze. Her earlier training was in organic synthesis and she felt wholly unprepared.
after: She writes that the time was not wasted. It was her first fieldwork in the ecosystem she hoped to study. She went on to run bigger and more expensive experiments that were becoming her dissertation chapters when she wrote the piece.
reflection: She describes having to tell an undergraduate helper, again and again, that she did not know what to do next.

sources.label: How my science ended up in the trash
sources.publisher: EcoPress, Natural Resource Ecology Laboratory, Colorado State University, undated

name: Harry Rolf
setback: A year and a half into his PhD at the University of Tasmania, Harry Rolf had to change his research focus and his supervisors after problems with supervision, funding and data. He had no scholarship, went part time and worked many jobs. His meeting records kept noting major concerns about a lack of tangible outputs.
after: His candidature was extended four times. He submitted in June 2016, two months after a meeting that again recorded those concerns, and the examiners asked only for minor corrections. He graduated after eight years.
reflection: He writes that managing his own expectations was his biggest challenge, and that it is rare for students to share stories like his.

sources.label: Reflection on my PhD experience- Harry Rolf
sources.publisher: Council of Australian Postgraduate Associations, September 2017

name: Zelalem Gurmessa
setback: Zelalem Gurmessa was studying at the University of KwaZulu-Natal on an Ethiopian government scheme when the funding was abandoned in 2013. He was paid only now and then until 2016. Then political unrest in Ethiopia made his planned data collection almost impossible.
after: He covered basic living costs with part-time lecturing and work as a postgraduate assistant. In 2016 he changed his topic to academic brain drain at African universities, and he submitted his thesis in November 2018.
reflection: He lost his funding and then his research plan, both for reasons far outside his control. He credits the people around him for getting through.

sources.label: Doctoral Graduate Changes Focus Midstream and Still Succeeds!
sources.publisher: University of KwaZulu-Natal, College of Law and Management Studies, 2019

name: Orin Robinson
setback: As a first-year PhD student at Rutgers University, Orin Robinson spent the spring and summer of 2010 trapping foxes on a barrier island to learn why they were eating shorebirds. He stored the specimens in his lab freezer. Then he learned the freezer had been unplugged for days, and every sample was ruined.
after: Starting again would have put him a year behind. He chose instead to do a theoretical study using data other people had collected. Eight years later most of his work was still theoretical, and he was a quantitative ecologist at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology.
reflection: One unplugged freezer ended a whole season of work and changed the kind of ecologist he became.

sources.label: That sinking feeling

name: Harvinder Virk
setback: Harvinder Virk's PhD on asthma relied on an antibody meant to stain a protein called TRPA1. After months of checks he found it was staining an unrelated protein. His early findings from patient biopsies were not valid, and none of the five antibodies on the market worked. He writes that he felt guilty and briefly considered leaving academia.
after: He published his validation results as the first paper of his PhD and changed course to study TRPA1 in more reliable ways. He became a clinical lecturer in respiratory medicine at the University of Leicester, and his team won a small grant to study the antibody problem.
reflection: He writes that he still feels guilty about the time and resources that were lost.

sources.label: Tales of the unexpected
sources.publisher: ASBMB Today, April 2023 (first published in eLife)

name: Nicole Aponte Santiago
setback: About a year into a PhD built on fruit flies, Nicole Aponte Santiago started feeling ill after time in the fly room. She grew more tired and struggled to concentrate. An allergy test confirmed that she had become allergic to the animal her whole project depended on, and she feared having to abandon it.
after: Her lab and institute gave her equipment and accommodations, and she planned experiments to spend as little time as possible in the fly room. She had her thesis data by the first lockdown in 2020. For her postdoc she chose to study neurons in zebrafish.
reflection: She found other fly researchers with the same allergy online, which is how she learned it could be managed.

sources.label: Tales of the unexpected
sources.publisher: ASBMB Today, April 2023 (first published in eLife)

name: Dominik Refardt
setback: Minutes after handing in his thesis on water fleas and their parasites, Dominik Refardt looked at control samples that should have been uninfected and saw parasite spores. An unknown parasite had got into many of his samples over four years of work. He asked for his thesis back and told his brother he was not sure he could graduate.
after: Going back through years of lab notes, he worked out that the intruder was a parasite new to science. He cut some results from the thesis, resubmitted and defended it. His former group later tracked the parasite down and he is a co-author on that paper. He now leads a research group.
reflection: His first impulse, he admits, was to tell no one. He went to a friend in the lab instead and said everything at once.

sources.label: When your PhD (almost) falls apart

name: Justin Chen
setback: Justin Chen spent six years on a biology PhD at MIT, working very long weeks while experiments often failed. Halfway through he realized he preferred writing to doing experiments. In the second half he had bouts of fatigue lasting a week at a time and withdrew from people. His lab shrank to two scientists as funding ran short.
after: He defended his thesis and stayed in the lab a few more months. His four-year relationship ended. He moved into science writing and communications, and was working at OpenBiome when the essay appeared.
reflection: He looks back on his younger self with compassion. He writes about the obsession, the isolation and the moments of wonder together.

sources.label: Coming to terms with six years in science: obsession, isolation, and moments of wonder

name: Matthew Gamble
setback: Matthew Gamble's PhD topic at the University of Manchester had not been defined before he started. He says he spent the first year and a half working out what he was doing, went down blind alleys and had to backtrack, and worried about whether he was on the right course.
after: He completed the PhD in 2014 and took a twelve-month postdoctoral contract in the same lab, which he called the path of least resistance. He expected to return to industry afterwards and was very wary of an academic career.
reflection: He finished, and he was still unsure academia was for him. Both were true when he was interviewed.

sources.label: The PhD experience: this far, and no further

name: Billy Jones
setback: Billy Jones, a PhD candidate at Lund University, had spent months organizing a first field trip to Kenya for April 2020, meant to be the foundation of his research. Kenya closed its borders in March. He had to rethink the whole project while caring for his toddler at home, and he describes the period as disabling.
after: He settled on a short-term plan, writing a historical account of a region in northern Kenya, and found that a single focus helped. When he wrote, he hoped to return to fieldwork once travel reopened. The post does not say how the PhD turned out.
reflection: His brother told him it was acceptable not to be productive during a pandemic. He writes that he was only beginning to take that in.

sources.label: Reflections from a PhD candidate and a Dad trying too hard during a Pandemic
sources.publisher: Lund University, Agenda 2030 Graduate School blog, May 2020

name: Emma Lawrence
setback: During her immunology PhD at the University of Manchester, Emma Lawrence came to doubt that academic science was for her. She found many experiments menial, resented how much luck decided who got good papers, and took the bad days personally. Near the end of her second year she concluded it was not worth it.
after: She completed the PhD in autumn 2012. After a spell in an office job and travelling, she became a project manager at Imperial College London. She says she will always wonder how life might have gone had she stayed.
reflection: She knows some people would say she gave up. She did not want to drift into the next step if it was not what she wanted.

sources.label: The PhD experience: this far, and no further

name: Anne-Wil Harzing
setback: After four years of part-time work on her PhD in the Netherlands, Anne-Wil Harzing opened a letter on a graduation day saying two of her three examiners had not approved it. Their comments implied rewriting it and cutting about half. An appeal stalled for five months and she dropped it. The delay cost her a subsidy for the ceremony costs.
after: A year later she submitted substantively the same manuscript at her new employer in the UK. It was approved without changes and she graduated in 1998. It was a finalist for two dissertation awards and was published as a book. She is now an emerita professor.
reflection: She kept the story private for nearly thirty years, and writes that the feeling of shame never fully left her.

sources.label: On failures in academia: My PhD journey
My PhD - a story that almost didn't end well

name: Aditi S. Iyengar
setback: Two months into her PhD in New Orleans, Aditi Iyengar's father died and she thought about staying home in India. In her third year she started a project from scratch, and after three months nothing was working. In her fourth year she spent months cleaning up a previous student's mistake, afraid her data were wrong.
after: Her mother urged her to finish, and she returned to school two weeks after the funeral. She wrote the essay in the final year of her PhD. Her author note says she went on to postdoctoral research at Massachusetts General Hospital.
reflection: Her mentor told her that most of the next few years would be failure. She was in tears in his office at the time.

sources.label: I am a Ph.D. student, and I’m a survivor

name: Meheli Banerjee
setback: Meheli Banerjee spent the first two and a half years of her PhD at the University of Eastern Finland on experiments and analysis before writing her first manuscript. The first journal rejected it without review. The second rejected it as well. A third, which she was sure was a good fit, rejected it too, and she writes that this one hurt a lot.
after: About three and a half years in, she spent hours reading about why papers and grants get rejected and how people cope, and turned it into a blog post with three diagrams. The post does not say whether the paper has been accepted. Her grant applications have brought many rejections and two acceptances.
reflection: She writes that her heart sinks in a familiar way every time an email ends with unfortunately. Getting used to it has not happened yet.

sources.label: Meheli Banerjee: Turning Nos into Next: surviving academic rejection one submission at a time
sources.publisher: University of Eastern Finland, Neuro-Innovation PhD programme, January 2026

name: Davina Robson
setback: Davina Robson, a PhD student at the University of Wollongong, waited months for reviews of her first article. One of three reviewers rejected it outright, so she rewrote it and moved to a second journal, where the same thing happened. The third asked for so many changes, some of which she did not agree with or understand, that she wanted to withdraw it.
after: She made the revisions as a last push. The article was accepted by a highly ranked journal in psychology and education.
reflection: She thought the second rejection would break her. She calls getting published an epic battle, harder than the writing.

sources.label: Trials and tribulations of higher study (and why it’s all worthwhile)

name: Sidney Altman
setback: He spent eighteen months as a physics graduate student at Columbia University. He writes that he was waiting unhappily for a chance to work in a laboratory and wondering whether he should stay in physics at all. He left the programme.
after: Eight months later, while working and taking a summer physics course in Colorado, he enrolled as a graduate student in biophysics at the University of Colorado Medical Center under Leonard Lerman. He writes that there he came to enjoy molecular biology.
reflection: A year and a half of waiting and wondering, then leaving. The second start was in a different field and a different city.

sources.label: Sidney Altman – Biographical
sources.publisher: NobelPrize.org, autobiography for the 1989 Nobel Prize

name: César Milstein
setback: He did his doctoral work in Buenos Aires with no economic support. He and his wife Celia both worked part-time in clinical biochemistry, earning just enough between them to keep going. He also describes himself as not a particularly brilliant student.
after: When the thesis on the enzyme aldehyde dehydrogenase was finished, he won a British Council Fellowship to the University of Cambridge, where he began collaborating with Fred Sanger.
reflection: A thesis paid for by two part-time jobs is still a thesis. Many people do their research in the hours left over from earning a living.

sources.label: César Milstein – Biographical
sources.publisher: NobelPrize.org, autobiography for the 1984 Nobel Prize

name: John C. Harsanyi
setback: He reached Sydney at the end of 1950, after fleeing Hungary, already holding a Hungarian doctorate in philosophy. His Hungarian degrees were not recognised and his English was poor, so for most of three years he did factory work and took economics courses in the evenings.
after: He received an M.A. in economics from the University of Sydney late in 1953 and became a lecturer at the University of Queensland in 1954. A Rockefeller Fellowship later took him to Stanford, where he earned a Ph.D. in economics.
reflection: Starting again as a student, after a degree that no longer counted, in a second language and after a shift on the factory floor.

sources.label: John C. Harsanyi – Biographical
sources.publisher: NobelPrize.org, autobiography for the 1994 Nobel Prize

name: Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard
setback: Her first thesis project, comparing the DNA of small phages, was given up once it became clear it would mostly mean refining techniques with uncertain success. By the end of her thesis in 1973 she writes that she had grown bored with her projects.
after: She finished with a different project on RNA polymerase, which was published as a letter in Nature. Then she read and asked around about developmental biology, and in 1975 moved to Basel as a postdoc to work on flies. She writes that it was hard to be a beginner in everything again.
reflection: A first project abandoned, and boredom at the end of the second one. Both are in her own account of her doctorate.

sources.label: Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard – Biographical
sources.publisher: NobelPrize.org, autobiography for the 1995 Nobel Prize

name: Yoshinori Ohsumi
setback: As a graduate student in Tokyo he writes that he was unable to produce particularly interesting results. Student protests pulled his attention from the lab, he moved to Kyoto and back during his doctorate, and he says he barely managed to finish a thesis.
after: Academic jobs were hard to get, so he went to a lab at The Rockefeller University in a very different field and felt very uncertain. He started his own lab at the University of Tokyo years later, with himself as its only member, and began his work on protein degradation at 43.
reflection: He describes his own doctorate as a thesis barely finished and results that were not especially interesting.

sources.label: Yoshinori Ohsumi – Biographical
sources.publisher: NobelPrize.org, autobiography for the 2016 Nobel Prize

name: Richard R. Ernst
setback: His doctoral work in Zürich was on using random noise in nuclear magnetic resonance. No experiments were attempted, he and his mentor did not believe the idea was useful, and he finished in 1962 feeling like a tightrope artist with no one interested in watching. He decided to leave the university for good.
after: He took an industry job at Varian in California. In 1964 he and Weston Anderson did the first pulse experiments that led to Fourier transform NMR. The paper was rejected twice by one journal before another accepted it, and Varian resisted building the instrument.
reflection: He ended his doctorate convinced nobody cared about the work, and he left. Wanting an audience for what you do is a reasonable thing to want.

sources.label: Richard R. Ernst – Biographical
sources.publisher: NobelPrize.org, autobiography for the 1991 Nobel Prize

name: Elinor Ostrom
setback: The economics department at UCLA discouraged her from a Ph.D. in economics, since she had no mathematics, having been advised as a girl not to take it. Political science admitted her with three other women in a class of 40, and they were later told the faculty had held a heated meeting criticising the decision to admit any women.
after: Her fellow students were friendly and encouraged the women to stay. She studied how a groundwater basin in Southern California was managed and defended her dissertation in 1965. Indiana University later appointed her to teach an introductory class at 7:30 in the morning.
reflection: She was let in through a side door and then told that some people had argued against opening it. She stayed in the room anyway.

sources.label: Elinor Ostrom – Biographical
sources.publisher: NobelPrize.org, autobiography for the 2009 Nobel Prize

name: Andre Geim
setback: In the first year of his PhD his supervisor moved to another institute 200 metres away, which meant losing some equipment and setting everything up again. Basic materials were scarce. His enthusiasm faded as he realised that no one, except perhaps his supervisor, was interested in what he was doing.
after: Looking back, he calls those five years remarkably uneventful in terms of science, and says they mattered mainly for the experimental skills he built with very little equipment.
reflection: Five years on a topic that almost nobody else cared about. He says so plainly, and does not pretend the thesis was more than it was.

sources.label: Andre Geim – Biographical
sources.publisher: NobelPrize.org, autobiography for the 2010 Nobel Prize

name: Martin Karplus
setback: A couple of months into graduate school at Caltech he gave a seminar to Max Delbrück's biology group. Delbrück kept interrupting to say he did not understand, and after half an hour the introduction was still not finished. Delbrück walked out, and later told him it was the worst seminar he had ever heard.
after: Karplus writes that he was devastated. The department chairman suggested finding another biology advisor, but he asked to transfer to chemistry instead. His advisor there, Kirkwood, left for Yale in 1951, so he moved to Linus Pauling and finished his thesis in 1953.
reflection: One bad afternoon in front of the group ended his first choice of field. It is hard to keep a single talk in proportion when you are new.

sources.label: Martin Karplus – Biographical
sources.publisher: NobelPrize.org, autobiography for the 2013 Nobel Prize

name: Oliver Smithies
setback: At Oxford he spent two years on a thesis problem and never reached the part he had been asked to solve. Half the thesis was thermodynamic equations in which he later found a fatal flaw, so they were never published. The other half became a paper that, he says, was never cited by him or by anyone else.
after: He went on to a postdoctoral fellowship at the University of Wisconsin. He writes that he thoroughly enjoyed the two years of trying, and that the work reinforced his habit of following experiments to the end regardless of how long they take.
reflection: A thesis with a flaw in one half and an uncited paper from the other. He tells this cheerfully, as a simple fact about how his doctorate went.

sources.label: Oliver Smithies – Biographical
sources.publisher: NobelPrize.org, autobiography for the 2007 Nobel Prize

name: John Clauser
setback: At Columbia, students needed a B or better in five key courses. He says he flunked quantum mechanics twice. His first thesis plan, a radio telescope flown on a U2 aircraft, was dropped. When he became interested in testing quantum mechanics, his advisor and the physics faculty told him he was nuts.
after: He completed a different thesis, measuring the cosmic microwave background through interstellar cyanide. As a graduate student he came across John Bell's paper, which he says started his whole career, and he later ran the experiment at Berkeley.
reflection: He still says he does not understand quantum mechanics. The course he failed twice was the subject he spent his life testing.

sources.label: Transcript from an interview with John Clauser
sources.publisher: NobelPrize.org, interview for the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics

name: Mary-Claire King
setback: In the late 1960s, early in her PhD at UC Berkeley, her experiments kept failing and she was on the brink of leaving. She had an attractive offer to work with Ralph Nader's new organisation in Washington. Having come from statistics, she doubted her ability to do experiments well.
after: Allan Wilson, who became her PhD mentor, encouraged her to stay and to design relatively simple experiments whose data she could interpret with her mathematics. Their project showed that humans and chimpanzees are 99% identical in their protein-coding sequences.
reflection: The experiments were not working and a good job elsewhere was on the table. Doubting your hands at the bench is common among people who arrive from another field.

sources.label: Mary-Claire King: Genetics as a Way of Thinking

name: Werner Heisenberg
setback: At his doctoral oral exam in Munich on 23 July 1923 he could not derive the resolving power of a telescope or a microscope, or say how a storage battery works. The experimentalist Wilhelm Wien saw no reason to pass him. After an argument among the examiners he received a low passing grade, and he was mortified.
after: He left the party held for him early and took the midnight train to Göttingen, where he asked Max Born whether the job he had been offered still stood. Born looked over the questions and kept the offer. A later attempt to teach him experimental physics was given up.
reflection: He left his own celebration and got on a night train. The shame of a bad exam can feel much larger than the exam.

sources.label: The Sad Story of Heisenberg's Doctorate
sources.publisher: American Institute of Physics, Heisenberg Web Exhibit

sources.label: The Sad Story of Heisenberg's Doctoral Oral Exam

name: Kamala Sohonie
setback: With a first-class degree from Bombay University, she applied to the Indian Institute of Science as a research student in biochemistry. The director, C. V. Raman, denied her entry because she was a woman. Only after great persistence from her and her family was she admitted in 1933, with restrictions the Institute's own magazine calls humiliating.
after: She left the Institute in 1936 and earned a PhD at Cambridge in 1939. Years later she said publicly that she could never forget how she had been treated.
reflection: She got in, did the work, and went on to a doctorate. She also never forgot the insult, and both things were true.

sources.label: Women and the Institute
sources.publisher: Connect with IISc, Indian Institute of Science, June 2018

name: Rob Bemthuis
setback: His PhD defence at the University of Twente had already been postponed several times. On the morning of the new date, 3 May 2024, while he was getting dressed, he learned that his supervisor Paul Havinga had died that morning. His other supervisor had advanced cancer and a hospital appointment that day.
after: He first wanted to cancel, then went ahead. Colleagues worked to make the defence legally valid, and his second supervisor, Maria Iacob, arrived in time to give the closing speech. She died that October. He is now an assistant professor at Twente.
reflection: He says the defence went by on autopilot. Some days in a PhD are simply got through, with other people holding things up.

sources.label: The human legacy of two special promotors

name: Corina Tarnita
setback: After winning Romania's national mathematics olympiad three years running, she went to Harvard and straight into its graduate school in pure mathematics. There her interest in mathematics was flickering and close to burning out. She was weighing a well-paid job at a bank or taking time off.
after: In the library she found a book on evolutionary dynamics by Martin Nowak, who was also at Harvard, and emailed him the same week she had to decide on the job. She turned the job down, finished her doctorate with him, and joined the Princeton faculty in 2013.
reflection: Losing interest in the subject you were always best at is its own kind of crisis. She stayed in research, but not in the field she started in.

sources.label: A Mathematician Who Decodes the Patterns Stamped Out by Life

name: Terence Tao
setback: He nearly failed his oral qualifying exam at Princeton, which he has put down to overconfidence and lack of preparation. The examiners passed him but told him his harmonic analysis was far from satisfactory. Afterwards his adviser, Elias Stein, sat him down and told him gently that the performance was a disappointment.
after: Tao has written that this was what he needed to hear, and that he began to work properly so as not to disappoint his adviser again. He completed his Princeton PhD in 1996.
reflection: Even a student who had been ahead all his life had an exam go badly, and a hard conversation after it.

sources.label: Math maestro Terence Tao *96 is solving the world’s puzzles
Terry Tao's generals

name: Brian May
setback: He began research on the zodiacal light, sunlight scattered by dust in the solar system, in 1970, and recorded more than 250 scans with a spectrometer in Tenerife in 1971 and 1972. Then the thesis was left unfinished for about 30 years while he played guitar in the band Queen.
after: He completed the research and thesis in 2007 and received his doctorate from Imperial College London that August. The thesis was published as a book in 2008.
reflection: The thesis sat unfinished for three decades while he did something else entirely, and it was still there when he came back.

sources.label: Brian May, guitarist for rock band Queen, completes Ph.D. thesis following 30-year hiatus
Queen's Guitarist Publishes Astrophysics Thesis

name: Benjamin Z. Houlton
setback: In the second year of his PhD his committee asked him to build a mathematical model of how climate shapes the nitrogen cycle around the planet. He had never built a model from scratch. The model crashed, giving the same result whatever he changed, and two months went by with no progress. He began to fear it would derail his dissertation and that his committee would judge him.
after: He asked a fellow graduate student with stronger coding skills for help. Together they found that the code was missing a full stop. Once he put full stops in the right places, the model worked and his dissertation moved forward. When the profile appeared he was a dean at Cornell University.
reflection: Two months lost to a missing full stop. The fear he describes was real even though the cause turned out to be small.

sources.label: Faculty Who Failed Series: Benjamin Z. Houlton

name: Corrie Moreau
setback: During her doctorate at Harvard her family was in crisis. Her mother was not well and her brother had been seriously injured, and once or twice a year she had to fly home at short notice to help. For the first two or three years she told no one, fearing that advisors and peers would think she was not committed to her research.
after: When she finally told her advisors and peers, she felt a great weight lift. Most were supportive, and some then shared struggles of their own. When the profile appeared she was a professor of entomology and a senior associate dean at Cornell University.
reflection: She carried it alone for years because she thought it would count against her. Hiding it was exhausting in itself.

sources.label: Faculty Who Failed Series: Corrie Moreau

name: Kehilwe Nakedi
setback: Nineteen years passed between the start of her university studies and her doctorate. Her university withheld her BSc certificate over unpaid fees, so she unwillingly spent five years in a non-scientific job to save for an honours degree. Later she worked as a research technologist to fund her postgraduate studies.
after: She began her PhD at the University of Cape Town in 2013 and published seven papers during it. She says it is extremely hard to focus on doing well when you are worried about rent and about going to bed hungry.
reflection: She would tell her 15-year-old self to be kind to herself, because she was doing the best she could with the cards she had been dealt.

sources.label: Commitment, passion and dogged determination
sources.publisher: UCT News, University of Cape Town, 12 December 2018

name: Gladys West
setback: She decided to pursue a PhD late in a long career as a Navy mathematician, at an age when most of her peers had retired, and finished the coursework before retiring so she could write the dissertation afterwards. After she retired she had a stroke. She recalls sitting at the computer when everything suddenly started spinning.
after: She says that after leaving hospital the thought came to her that she could not stay in bed and had to get up and finish the PhD. Her thesis, on the effects of downsizing on the employees who remain, is dated 2000.
reflection: She asked herself whether she still had it in her to do it. The question was open when she started, and again after the stroke.

sources.label: Gladys West: In her own words
sources.publisher: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews
